card.stem: Lifetime use of a dwelling should be a key consideration at the design stage.
card.questionText: Using notes and freehand sketches, discuss two best-practice guidelines that should be followed when designing for lifetime use at each of the following areas of a dwelling: entrance access.

rows.contextNote: First guideline for the entrance access: notes 4 and sketches 4. card.stem: The sketch shows a railway keepers cottage built over 130 years ago. These traditional cottages can be seen at railway crossing points throughout our rural landscape. They form an important part of our built heritage.
card.questionText: A survey of the cottage reveals: 500 mm solid external wall of stone construction, uninsulated, with an internal lime render. Using notes and freehand sketches, describe in detail the steps involved in upgrading the thermal performance of each area selected in a manner that respects the original character of the cottage.

rows.verbatim: Steps involved in upgrading the thermal performance of each area selected
rows.contextNote: Notes on the steps for the stone wall, respecting the cottage’s character. Such as: keep the wall breathable, with layers more vapour-permeable towards the outside and no impermeable vapour barriers; use hygroscopic natural insulation (hemp/hempcrete, lime, wood fibre, cork, sheep’s wool); rake out and repoint with lime mortar by hand (joints raked to twice their width, dampened first, filled in stages, protected with hessian while it carbonates); apply hempcrete internally and allow 4–6 weeks to dry, then lime render, or a three-coat lime plaster (scud coat, haired scratch coat, float coat, lime-putty finish).

card.stem: Shown in the sketch is the proposed external wall design detail for a new house of timber frame construction.
card.questionText: Calculate the U-value of the proposed wall, given the construction has the following sequence and data: External render thickness 16 mm External concrete block thickness 100 mm Clear cavity width 60 mm Oriented Strand Board (OSB) thickness 12 mm Timber stud thickness 250 mm Insulation between studs thickness 250 mm Oriented Strand Board (OSB) thickness 12 mm Plasterboard thickness 12.5 mm. Thermal data of the external wall: Resistance of external surface (R) 0.048 m2 ºC/W; Resistivity of external render (r) 2.170 m ºC/W; Conductivity of concrete block (k) 1.440 W/m ºC; Resistance of clear cavity (R) 0.440 m2 ºC/W; Conductivity of OSB (k) 0.130 W/m ºC; Conductivity of insulation (k) 0.039 W/m ºC; Conductivity of OSB (k) 0.130 W/m ºC; Conductivity of plasterboard (k) 0.250 W/m ºC; Resistance of internal surface (R) 0.130 m2 ºC/W. Note: The timber studs need not be considered in your calculations.

rows.contextNote: Set out the layers, thicknesses (in metres), k or r values and resistances in a table.
External surface resistance 0.048 and internal surface resistance 0.130 m²°C/W, 3 each.

Seven layer resistances, 3 each: render 0.016 × 2.170 = 0.035; concrete block 0.100 ÷ 1.440 = 0.069; clear cavity 0.440 (given); OSB 0.012 ÷ 0.130 = 0.092; insulation 0.250 ÷ 0.039 = 6.410; OSB 0.092; plasterboard 0.0125 ÷ 0.250 = 0.050 m²°C/W. The studs are ignored, as the question states.
Total resistance Rt = 7.367 m²°C/W (sum of all resistances).
U = 1 ÷ Rt = 1 ÷ 7.367 = 0.136 W/m²°C, with units.

Thermal data of the external wall: Resistance of external surface (R) 0.048 m2 ºC/W; Resistivity of external render (r) 2.170 m ºC/W; Conductivity of concrete block (k) 1.440 W/m ºC; Resistance of clear cavity (R) 0.440 m2 ºC/W; Conductivity of OSB (k) 0.130 W/m ºC; Conductivity of insulation (k) 0.039 W/m ºC; Conductivity of OSB (k) 0.130 W/m ºC; Conductivity of plasterboard (k) 0.250 W/m ºC; Resistance of internal surface (R) 0.130 m2 ºC/W. Note: The timber studs need not be considered in your calculations.

(b) Using the U-value of the wall obtained at 5(a) above and the following data, calculate the cost of heat lost annually through this wall: area of external wall 144 m2; average internal temperature 20 ºC; average external temperature 7 ºC; heating period 6 hours daily for 33 weeks per annum; cost of wood pellets 55 cent per kg; calorific value of wood pellets 17350 kJ per kg; 1000 watts 1 kJ per second.

(c) Using notes and freehand sketches, show the typical design detailing that will prevent the build-up of moisture within the timber frame structure.

rows.contextNote: Set out the layers, thicknesses (in metres), k or r values and resistances in a table.
External surface resistance 0.048 and internal surface resistance 0.130 m²°C/W, 3 each.

Seven layer resistances, 3 each: render 0.016 × 2.170 = 0.035; concrete block 0.100 ÷ 1.440 = 0.069; clear cavity 0.440 (given); OSB 0.012 ÷ 0.130 = 0.092; insulation 0.250 ÷ 0.039 = 6.410; OSB 0.092; plasterboard 0.0125 ÷ 0.250 = 0.050 m²°C/W. The studs are ignored, as the question states.
Total resistance Rt = 7.367 m²°C/W (sum of all resistances).
U = 1 ÷ Rt = 1 ÷ 7.367 = 0.136 W/m²°C, with units.
Heat loss = U × area × temperature difference = 0.136 × 144 × (20 − 7) = 254.592 W (J/s).
Heating time = 60 × 60 × 6 × 7 × 33 = 4,989,600 seconds per year.

rows.contextNote: Wood pellets = 1,270,312.243 ÷ 17,350 = 73.2168 kg per year.
Cost = 73.2168 × €0.55 = €40.27 per year. The single-formula method (U × area × ΔT × seconds × cost ÷ (calorific value × 1000)) gives the same €40.27.

Such as: a breather membrane on the outer face that lets vapour escape but sheds external water, with taped joints; a vapour control layer on the warm (inner) side, continuous and sealed at every lap, so warm humid air cannot reach the frame and cause interstitial condensation and rot.

card.stem: “It would be reasonable to assume that ensuring good indoor air quality would be a key factor when designing and constructing buildings. The term sick building syndrome became well known in the 1980’s and still lingers today, though largely associated with poorly air-conditioned offices. However, the health impacts of buildings are still poorly understood and rarely taken into account as a key priority when buildings are designed or renovated. Architects, when specifying building materials are mainly concerned with cost, availability, robustness and aesthetics, not their impacts on health.” Adapted from: Building Materials, Health and Indoor Air Quality: No Breathing Space by Tom Wooley
